purpose: Cross-tenant join of Firm Drop Down VALUES, to test (a) whether `isReadOnlyRecord` tracks provenance or reference count, and (b) whether the publish-and-fork model extends from page layouts to code tables.

theTestIProposedCouldNotRun.proposed: Find a value with the SAME LxBOID in both tenants but a DIFFERENT isReadOnlyRecord - that would prove reference-counting or per-tenant config.
theTestIProposedCouldNotRun.result: UNRUNNABLE. **Zero** (tableType, LxBOID) pairs are shared between the tenants - AF has 1,140 values and BBW 1,217, with completely disjoint id spaces.
theTestIProposedCouldNotRun.lesson: Same trap as the page layouts: ids are re-keyed per tenant, so an id-join yields a false negative. Joining on NAME is the correct test - the lesson team-lead drew from the layout join generalises.

conclusion.provenanceCONFIRMED: Observed, and decisive. Across **646** values sharing (tableType, name) in both tenants, `isReadOnlyRecord` agrees **646 out of 646** - not one disagreement. And of the **1,045** values unique to one tenant (477 AF-only, 568 BBW-only), **ZERO** are read-only. Every protected value exists in both tenants; every tenant-unique value is deletable. That is exactly what platform-seeded-versus-firm-added predicts.
conclusion.referenceCountingREFUTED: This kills the reference-count reading outright. The two tenants differ enormously in data volume - AF holds 2 contracts and 400 locations against BBW's 2,190 and 2,140, roughly a thousandfold difference on contracts. If `delete` were suppressed by rows referencing a value, the flag would have to differ somewhere across 646 shared values. It differs **nowhere**. A reference count cannot produce identical flags across tenants with a 1000x data difference.
conclusion.consequenceForD07: This closes it out. Lucernex is NOT performing a Where-Used reference check on code-table values, so Q-BBW-01 gives no grounds to reopen ASG Edge+ D-07 / MST-015. The earlier reading in bbw-vs-american-freight.md §3 is retracted and now has cross-tenant evidence against it, not merely a counterexample.
conclusion.publishAndForkEXTENDS: Derived. Code tables follow the SAME publish-and-fork pattern as page layouts: one seeded set (646 shared names, ~153 of them protected), re-keyed per tenant into disjoint id spaces, then forked locally with firm-added values (477 at AF, 568 at BBW - all editable). So the distribution models are now: page layouts and code tables PUBLISHED-THEN-FORKED; workflows TENANT-AUTHORED; navigation and the SQL table catalog PLATFORM-SEEDED AND SHARED (identical ids across tenants).

caveat: One AF value counts as read-only outside the 646 shared-name set because two values in one table share a name and collapse to a single key. It is not a counterexample to the pattern - just a duplicate-name artefact of the join.
